newsitem.title: USA: Fed's McDonough ties policy target/credibility.
newsitem.headline: Fed's McDonough ties policy target/credibility.

text.p: Announcing a target for monetary policy enhances the credibility of a central bank's commitment to price stability and helps lock in inflation expectations, Federal Reserve Bank of New York William McDonough said on Wednesday.

"While central bankers may differ in the ways they seek to achieve price stability ... the goal we all strive for is no less important," McDonough said in a prepared speech delivered before the Economic Club of New York.

"A goal of price stability requires that monetary policy be oriented beyond the horizon of its immediate impact on the inflation and the economy," McDonough said. "This immediate horizon is on the order of two to three years.
McDonough reminded the audience of Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's definition of price stability -- "when inflation is not a consideration in household and business decisions."

"What is critical in the operation of such a definition is that inflation expectations are anchored over the long term by some transparent commitment by the central bank to an articulated standard," McDonough stressed.

The New York Fed president was the first Fed official to propose a specific target for U.S. monetary policy in a March 21 speech. McDonough proposed targeting the U.S. Consumer Price Index in a range between 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent to account for the suspected bias in this broad inflation gauge.

Among the severe costs inflation inflicts on an economy, McDonough cited "the overinvestment in the financial sector," since "resources in high-inflation economies diverted from productive activities to non-productive financial transactions are enormous."
McDonough, however, cautioned against the high cost to an economy of trying to achieve price stability too quickly.
"Abrupt shifts in policy... especially a monetary tightening in the face of wages that are unlikely to be cut, can cause unacceptable rises in unemployment and drops in output," McDonough said.

"Rapid moves toward price stability from high inflation, however, do have their costs under certain circumstances," McDonough added, referring to "a rapid transfer of resources ... causing unemployment and business failures to follow -- what was boom, goes bust."
McDonough also pointed out that having price stability as a goal does not mean a central bank should ignore economic growth.

"Some would argue that establishing price stability as the primary goal of monetary policy means that central banks will no longer be concerned about output or growth," the New York Fed president said. "I believe this view is simply wrong."

While stressing price stability is the only way a central bank can contribute to long-term growth, McDonough said adopting "a (monetary policy) target is one proven means of credibly conveying to the public the commitment to price stability and thereby locking in inflation expectations.
McDonough noted central banks can target a certain foreign exchange rate, the monetary aggregates or inflation.
"A country that fixes its exchange rate surrenders control of its domestic monetary policy," he said.

Turning to the monetary aggregates, McDonough added that "the advantages of a monetary aggregate target are totally dependent upon the predictability of the relationship between the monetary target and the inflation goal."
"In the United States, these relationships are not sufficiently stable for the monetary targeting approach to work," he said.
McDonough said a third method for implementing monetary policy is inflation targeting.

"For countries that are unable or unwilling to fix their exchange rate to that of another country and cannot rely on stable relationships between monetary aggregates and goals, the inflation target approach offers a transparent means of commitment over the longer term," he said. "I believe that the inflation targeting approach to price stability merits further study and consideration."
